newsitem.title: UK: Cocoa nations may strike a deal on reserve fund.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa nations may strike a deal on reserve fund.

text.p: Cocoa nations, meeting in London next week, will try to settle differences over how much of buffer stock profits should be channelled to a reserve fund.
"We are trying to get a decision this time," said a delegate to the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO), an 36-member, mainly advisory group representing consumers and producers.
A five-day Council session starting on Monday, will be chaired by Guy-Alain Gauze, the Ivorian Commodities Minister.

Traders say, however, they may be sceptical over any Ivorian crop forecasts made in the lobbies, noting that the trade is at present ready for something around 1.1 million tonnes versus the government's 950,000.
Cocoa prices have recovered from a downtrend on the back of a technical rally in recent weeks but are vulnerable to perceptions that the Ivorian harvest may be near a record again.
While the ICCO meeting will be focused on house keeping and project reviews, delegates may ask Gauze what measures he has in mind for the midcrop and to curb the overall production.
But the spotlight of the talks will be the reserve fund.
Most members have agreed in principle to set up a fund to plug budget shortfalls when lucrative buffer stock sales end next year and to liquidate the existing cocoa agreement.

"The problem is that when the buffer stocks contribution finally disappears there will be a huge gap, something like 40 percent, in ICCO running costs," said Tim Mordan, the delegate for the UK and chairman of the ICCO executive committee.
But when it comes to the size of the fund, opinions differ wildly, even within producer and consumer camps.

A sticking point is how to allocate a last tranche of some $330 million expected to pile up in ICCO coffers from the sale of 250,000 tonnes of buffer stock cocoa by 1998. These were gathered through a levy system mostly charged on producers.
Most delegates, except Brazil, agreed to set aside some $4 million surplus profit expected from the sale of buffer stocks.
But Brazil blocked an agreement in December, saying it had already allocated its share of the buffer stock profits to fight witches' broom - a cocoa disease that has ravaged its crop.
Asked what his country's position would be next week, one Brazilian delegate said: "The position will be put at the meeting. We have not received the instructions from Brasilia."
A group of consumer country members met in Brussels on Thursday, but failed to find a common ground with their ideas ranging between a fund of 2.5 and four million pounds sterling.
Producers have thrown their weight behind executive director Eduard Kouame's proposal for 4-5 million stg. Some delegates said three million stg might be a compromise.

There are also divisions on the purpose of such a fund. Consumers said the objective should be a future liquidation of the present cocoa agreement but producers eyed generous interest earnings as a way to finance ICCO costs.
Monday's session will also feature a presentation by the President of Japan's Chocolate and Cocoa Association, Akira Sasai, on the development of consumption in Japan.

Other items on the agenda include a discussion on the fate of the ICCO's mammoth $14 million cocoa tree stock project which is struggling to find the necessary funding after rejection by the UN Common Fund for Commodities in December.
With no additional money the project is now stalled, but ICCO countries are still chasing other sources for finance.

The five producer countries that are taking part in the project to count all trees to monitor future production, were urged to reassess their priorities and streamline local costs which may have boosted the provisional estimates significantly.

There will also be talks on a new environmental project to which the Netherlands and Japan have pledged the initial money, and the European Union's directive allowing vegetable fats in chocolate, but no developments are expected on this.
